title: OpenAI’s latest math breakthroughs commit research misconduct, experts say
excerpt: OpenAI released 10 AI-generated results over the weekend. Some mathematicians are unhappy with their approach
content_html:
OpenAI’s newest chatbot may be a whiz at math, but it seems to be lagging far behind humans in its academic rigor.

Last week the company announced 10 more artificial-intelligence-generated math advances that were found during internal development and testing of its next major large language model. This batch of results came from that LLM, Astra, and each one resolves or progresses a different “long-standing open problem” of “substantial interest” to the mathematical community. The company said that the total token cost was a mere $2,000.

The news quickly spread as yet another harbinger of AI’s promise—or threat—of outpacing humans to become a dominant, disruptive force in math and computer science. But over the days following the announcement, as flesh-and-blood experts poured over the nearly 250-page paper in detail, many grew frustrated.

Two of the most exciting results, the experts say, incorporate preexisting ideas from the recent mathematical literature without properly citing them. This contradicts OpenAI’s initial press release, which said that the problems Astra addressed “have been open and seen no progress on the main result for at least a decade.” (OpenAI has since updated the language to be more accurate).

“They are running roughshod over the work of others who came before them in a deliberate way,” says Steven Miller, a mathematician at Yeshiva University, who argues that OpenAI has effectively plagiarized his own research. “It seems completely systematic to me, and it points to research misconduct.”

The result Miller refers to concerns how many balls you can fit in a box—a seemingly simple problem, except these balls and boxes exist in a mathematical space of 1,000 dimensions—or even more. OpenAI’s paper improves the best estimate for how tightly these balls can possibly be packed. The LLM-generated proof hinges on a particular mathematical argument that it presented as its own but that actually first appeared in a 2016 paper by Miller and a collaborator.

Another of the 10 results resolves a long-standing question in group theory, which studies sets of mathematical objects called “groups” that interact in an organized way. Mathematicians have long wondered whether all groups have a property called “soficity,” the capacity to be faithfully approximated in a particularly way by other, simpler groups. The OpenAI paper establishes at least one group that lacks this property.

The discovery stunned Francesco Fournier-Facio, a mathematician at the University of Cambridge, who studies group theory—at least until he “engaged with this breakthrough as I would if a human had written it,” he says. The result, he and some of his colleagues found, wasn’t as novel as it first appeared. Like a number of recent AI breakthroughs, it pasted together ideas from the mathematical literature to build a new theorem. Once again, the LLM’s trick is its superhuman patience for assembling puzzle pieces, not the ability to make some profound intellectual leap.

In particular, Astra’s key mathematical step combined ideas first found in two papers from 2016 and 2019. Andreas Thom, a mathematician at the Dresden University of Technology, who co-authored the 2019 paper, summarized the result on MathOverflow.com, calling it “creative and at the same time elementary.”*

OpenAI’s initial press release seemed to ignore—or be completely unaware of—these crucial, recent developments. Fournier-Facio argues that the two preceding papers show humans had not hit a stalemate with the soficity problem. OpenAI’s mathematicians did their best to attribute these ideas correctly in their paper, he says. But, in spite of their good intentions, “there is the big PR machine that wants to sound as impressive as possible and does not care about being 100 percent accurate,” he says.

“We take responsibility for the correctness of these results and are meeting the same standards generally expected of human mathematicians,” an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement to Scientific American. “We plan to make small updates [to the paper] this week, consistent with standard academic practice.”

But as AI continues its campaign to conquer math without any built-in fealty to the field’s academic norms, some in the community are clearly losing patience. “OpenAI is now fully participating in high-level research,” Fournier-Facio says. “So they should be held to the same academic standards that we are.”

*Editor’s Note (8/7/26): This sentence was edited after posting to correct the description of Andreas Thom co-authoring the 2019 paper.

content_html_zh:
OpenAI 最新的聊天机器人可能是数学高手，但在学术严谨性方面似乎远远落后于人类。

上周，该公司宣布了另外 10 项人工智能生成的数学进展，这些进展是在其下一个主要大型语言模型的内部开发和测试过程中发现的。 这批成果来自那个LLM、Astra，每一个都解决或推进了数学界“实质性兴趣”的不同“长期悬而未决的问题”。 该公司表示，代币总成本仅为 2,000 美元。

这一消息迅速传播开来，成为人工智能有望超越人类，成为数学和计算机科学领域的主导、颠覆性力量的又一个预兆。 但在宣布这一消息后的几天里，随着有血有肉的专家们详细地研读这份近 250 页的论文，许多人感到沮丧。

关于支持科学新闻

如果您喜欢这篇文章，请考虑通过订阅来支持我们屡获殊荣的新闻报道。 通过购买订阅，您将有助于确保有关塑造当今世界的发现和想法的影响力故事的未来。

专家们表示，其中两个最令人兴奋的结果融合了最近数学文献中先前存在的想法，但没有正确引用它们。 这与 OpenAI 最初的新闻稿相矛盾，该新闻稿称 Astra 解决的问题“一直是开放的，至少十年来在主要结果上没有任何进展”。 （OpenAI 此后更新了语言，使其更加准确）。

叶史瓦大学 (Yeshiva University) 数学家史蒂文·米勒 (Steven Miller) 表示：“他们故意粗暴对待前人的工作。”他认为 OpenAI 实际上抄袭了他自己的研究成果。 “在我看来，这完全是系统性的，它指出了研究不当行为。”

米勒提到的结果涉及一个盒子里可以装多少个球——一个看似简单的问题，但这些球和盒子存在于 1,000 维甚至更多维的数学空间中。 OpenAI 的论文改进了对这些球的包装紧密程度的最佳估计。 LLM 生成的证明取决于一个特定的数学论证，该论证是它自己提出的，但实际上首次出现在 Miller 和合作者 2016 年的一篇论文中。

10 个结果中的另一个解决了群论中一个长期存在的问题，群论研究称为“群”的数学对象集，它们以有组织的方式相互作用。 数学家长期以来一直想知道是否所有群都具有一种称为“社交性”的属性，即被其他更简单的群以特定方式忠实逼近的能力。 OpenAI 论文至少建立了一个缺乏这一属性的群体。

这一发现震惊了剑桥大学数学家弗朗西斯科·福尼耶-法西奥（Francesco Fournier-Facio），他研究群论——至少在他“像人类写下的那样参与这一突破之前是这样”，他说。 他和他的一些同事发现，结果并不像最初看起来那么新颖。 就像最近的许多人工智能突破一样，它融合了数学文献中的想法来构建一个新的定理。 再说一遍，法学硕士的秘诀在于它对拼凑拼图的超人耐心，而不是实现某些深刻的智力飞跃的能力。

特别是，Astra 的关键数学步骤结合了 2016 年和 2019 年两篇论文中首次发现的想法。 德累斯顿工业大学数学家 Andreas Thom 是 2019 年论文的合著者，他在 MathOverflow.com 上总结了这一结果，称其“富有创意，同时又很基本。”*

OpenAI 最初的新闻稿似乎忽略了——或者完全没有意识到——这些重要的最新进展。 福尼尔-法西奥认为，前两篇论文表明人类在社交问题上并未陷入僵局。 他说，OpenAI 的数学家尽了最大努力在论文中正确地解释了这些想法。 但是，尽管他们的意图是好的，“有一个大型公关机器希望听起来尽可能令人印象深刻，并不关心是否 100% 准确，”他说。

OpenAI 发言人在给《科学美国人》的一份声明中表示：“我们对这些结果的正确性负责，并达到了人类数学家普遍期望的相同标准。” “我们计划本周对[这篇论文]进行一些小更新，以符合标准的学术实践。”

但随着人工智能继续其征服数学的运动，而不对该领域的学术规范有任何内在的忠诚，社区中的一些人显然正在失去耐心。 “OpenAI 现在正在全面参与高水平研究，”Fournier-Facio 说。 “所以他们应该遵守与我们相同的学术标准。”

*编者注（8/7/26）：这句话是在发布后编辑的，以更正 Andreas Thom 共同撰写 2019 年论文的描述。
